posts.author: Priyanshu Chourasia
posts.title: Kafka: My journey from what it is to how it works
posts.content:
How I first heard about Kafka

I first heard about Kafka from a random YouTuber. According to them, Kafka is an event streaming platform that stores data for a set period of time, can handle heavy data ingestion, rarely breaks, and keeps applications that depend on real-time data moving. Back then, I didn't know it in any depth — I had only heard about it.


Why I thought of using it

Around the same time, there was a data persistence issue going on at my office. Whenever a race condition happened, our TCP server was unable to insert data into the database, and we were losing data packets.

So I thought of adding Kafka as a layer between the TCP server and the database. That way, the database would not have to open multiple connections, and if the database ever failed or ran out of space, at least I would still have the data.


That was my introduction to Kafka. Now I will take you into its depth. If I missed anything, you can mail me at the address in the footer or reach out to me on social media. Let's get into the deep architecture of Kafka.


What is Kafka? What is its formal definition?

Kafka is a distributed event streaming platform used to collect, store, process and move large volumes of real-time data between different applications and systems.


What is a distributed system, and why do we need one?

So the first question is: what is a distributed system? A small request — don't get bored. This is the warm-up needed to understand the system properly.

For a long time, applications ran on a single machine, which we can call the primary machine. When the internet became popular and the number of users grew, that single machine became hard to manage. It became a single point of failure: if the primary machine failed under load, users had no other point of access. Scaling the application also became difficult. Then came the ideas of vertical scaling and horizontal scaling.


Scaling, explained with a New Year party

An easy way to remember what scaling is: imagine you are hosting a New Year party and you print only 40 invitation cards. As news of your party spreads, more people ask you for an invite, and they are even willing to pay. So you expand the guest list to 150.

Now the bigger problem is that your house doesn't have the capacity for that many people. Even your cook complains that they need more helpers and more ingredients to prepare the food. So instead of taking the invites back, you ask a friend whether you can scale, and you offer to pay for the place. Your friend says, "Yes, of course," and lets you set up the party in their field, which can hold more than 150 people. This is what scaling looks like in real life.


Vertical scaling

Now suppose more than 150 people turn up — say 190. You were already prepared for this, because you moved out of the place that held 40 people and rented one that holds 150 and more. That is vertical scaling: making the one place bigger.


Horizontal scaling

Then you turn this party into a business. You rent fields in multiple cities to host parties, and you even send invites to 600 people in the same city. Instead of growing one field from 200 to 600 people, you rent multiple properties to host them. That is horizontal scaling: adding more places instead of making one place bigger.


So what is a distributed system?

A distributed system can be understood as multiple computers holding data in a distributed manner, while appearing as one single system to users. Instead of relying on one big, massive server, the data is distributed across multiple independent computers. There are no shared resources, because every system has its own CPU, memory and processes.

Now the question comes: how do these computers communicate, and how are their connections maintained? We will try to find that out in another blog. Up to this point, you have understood what scaling is, the types of scaling, and what a distributed system is.


A distributed system, explained with a toy factory

Imagine you own a toy factory. Instead of depending on one factory to manufacture toys and deliver them to every other city, you set up one factory near Delhi and another in Maharashtra, so each one can deliver to the states nearby. And if one factory ever goes down because of a technical fault, the other will continue to run and serve.


Back to Kafka: what is event streaming?

Now read the definition of Kafka again: a distributed event streaming platform. We know what distributed means, so what is event streaming? Kafka's own website defines it like this:

Event streaming is the digital equivalent of the human body’s central nervous system. It is the technological foundation for the ‘always-on’ world where businesses are increasingly software-defined and automated, and where the user of software is more software.
— Apache Kafka website

In simpler words, an event stream is an ordered sequence of events representing actions that happened. When you visited my site and clicked this article to read it, that click was an event — one I can capture to count how many people visited my Kafka article. Then you upvoted the article, meaning you liked it. That is another event, and it happened after you opened the article. This is how I can build a dashboard with charts showing how many people clicked and how many liked it.


Event stream processing (ESP)

Event stream processing (ESP) takes a continuous stream of events and processes them as soon as they happen. In the example I just gave, every change can be recorded as an event, with the events ordered by time — what happened, and when. These events are then pushed and handled one at a time, which gives the system real-time updates instead of processing them in batches.


The communication model: publish and subscribe

Kafka uses the publish–subscribe communication model. So what is this communication model, and what roles does it have?

The publish–subscribe pattern is an asynchronous messaging architectural pattern. The senders of events are called publishers, and the receivers of messages are called subscribers. The two are decoupled through a central intermediary called a message broker.

So the core components are: publishers, subscribers, the message broker, and the topic (or channel).

Why is this important to understand? Because the concepts of this communication model are what helped Kafka build an architecture that lets millions of software systems persist their data and transfer it in real time.

What are the benefits of this model?

Decoupling: publishers and subscribers do not depend on each other, and they don't need any knowledge of each other. Every part just has its own role to play.

Asynchronous communication: this is one more important part. Publishers do not wait for a response, or for a subscriber to be online. A publisher just drops the message and continues processing.

Kafka combines three key capabilities:

  1. To publish (write) and subscribe to (read) streams of events, including continuous import/export of your data.
  2. To store streams of events durably and reliably for as long as you want.
  3. To process streams of events as they occur, or retrospectively.

A cluster is a unified group of multiple servers, called nodes, that work together as if they were a single system.

*Note: a peer is a person who is of the same age or position in society as you.

What is a broker in Kafka?

A server on which Kafka is deployed and running is called a broker. So, for a real distributed system, if you install Kafka on 5 servers, you have 5 brokers.

Now let's try to understand how these brokers work.

posts.author: Priyanshu Chourasia
posts.title: How to buy a CPU: what questions must be asked?
posts.desc: Cores, GHz, cache, TDP, sockets — a practical list of the questions to ask before buying a CPU, so you pay for the performance you'll actually use.
posts.intro: Most bad CPU purchases don't come from picking a weak chip — they come from skipping a question. Here's the list I go through before buying one.
posts.content:
Why a CPU is harder to buy than it looks. A CPU spec sheet throws a dozen numbers at you — cores, threads, GHz, cache, TDP, socket — and the product names change every year. Most bad CPU purchases don't come from picking a weak chip; they come from skipping a question. Here are the questions I ask, in the order I ask them.


1. What will I actually use it for?

This is the question that decides everything else. Write down your top two or three workloads honestly, not aspirationally.

  • Office, browsing, light coding — almost any modern 4–6 core chip is enough. Spend the money on an SSD and RAM instead.
  • Gaming — games care more about strong per-core speed and large cache than about high core counts. 6–8 fast cores is the sweet spot.
  • Compiling, video editing, 3D rendering, VMs, Docker — these scale with cores. 12–16+ cores pay for themselves here.
  • Local AI / ML — the GPU usually matters far more than the CPU; don't overspend on the processor at the GPU's expense.

2. What is my total budget — for the whole platform?

A CPU never comes alone. Price the CPU + motherboard + RAM + cooler together. A cheaper CPU on an expensive platform can cost more than a better CPU on a sensible one. A good rule: if the CPU eats so much budget that you're forced into a weak GPU or 8 GB of RAM, you picked the wrong CPU.


3. Intel or AMD — and which socket?

Brand loyalty is less useful than asking: what socket does this use, and how long will that socket be supported? A socket with a long upgrade path means you can drop in a faster CPU in three years without replacing the motherboard. Check the motherboard's chipset too — the same socket can have chipsets that disable overclocking, limit PCIe lanes, or need a BIOS update before they recognise a newer CPU.


4. How many cores and threads do I really need?

More cores only help if your software uses them. Ask: does my main workload scale across cores (rendering, compiling, encoding) or does it lean on a few fast ones (most games, many desktop apps)? Also be aware that many modern chips mix performance cores and efficiency cores — a "14-core" CPU might have only 6 full-speed cores. Read the breakdown, not just the total.


5. Is clock speed (GHz) comparable across chips?

Only within the same generation and architecture. A newer CPU at 4.5 GHz can easily beat an older one at 5.0 GHz because it does more work per clock (IPC). Look at the boost clock for single-thread tasks, but always confirm with real benchmarks for the software you use rather than comparing GHz numbers.


6. How much cache does it have?

L3 cache is one of the most underrated specs. Large caches dramatically help gaming and some data-heavy workloads because the CPU waits less on RAM. Chips with extra stacked cache often beat "faster" chips in games for exactly this reason.


7. Does it have integrated graphics?

If you're not buying a graphics card — or want a backup display output when troubleshooting — make sure the CPU has an iGPU. Some model variants (for example Intel's "F" SKUs) ship without one, and that saves money only if you already have a GPU.


8. How much power does it draw, and can I cool it?

Check the TDP / base power and, more importantly, the maximum turbo power. A chip that boosts to 250 W needs a serious cooler, a good motherboard VRM, and a decent power supply. Ask whether a cooler is included in the box, and whether the stock cooler is actually adequate or just a placeholder. For laptops and small builds, a lower-power chip that stays at its boost clock beats a hotter chip that throttles.


9. What memory and I/O does the platform support?

  • RAM type — DDR4 or DDR5? Newer platforms may be DDR5-only, which changes your RAM cost.
  • PCIe version and lanes — matters if you want fast NVMe SSDs or multiple drives alongside a GPU.
  • USB, Thunderbolt, Wi-Fi — some of this comes from the CPU/chipset, so check before you assume.

10. Am I going to overclock?

If not, don't pay extra for unlocked chips (Intel "K", certain AMD models) and overclocking-class motherboards. If yes, budget for the matching chipset and better cooling — an unlocked CPU on a locked board is wasted money.


11. Is the previous generation a better deal?

Right after a new launch, last-generation CPUs often drop in price and deliver 85–90% of the performance for much less. Ask: what does the new generation actually add for my workload? If the answer is "5% in benchmarks I don't run," buy the older one.


12. Where am I buying it, and what's the warranty?

Buy boxed retail from an authorised seller when possible. Check warranty length and whether it's handled by the seller or the manufacturer. For used CPUs, ask about overclocking history, check for bent pins (or pads on LGA sockets), and test it before the return window closes.


A quick checklist before you click "Buy"

  • Workload written down, and benchmarks checked for that workload.
  • Total platform cost (CPU + board + RAM + cooler) fits the budget.
  • Socket and chipset confirmed compatible — BIOS version checked.
  • Core breakdown (P-cores vs E-cores) understood.
  • Cooler and PSU can handle the max turbo power.
  • iGPU present if you need it.
  • Previous-gen alternative priced and compared.
  • Warranty and seller verified.
posts.footer: There's no single "best CPU" — only the best CPU for your workload, budget, and platform. Ask these questions in order, check real benchmarks for the software you actually use, and you'll rarely regret the purchase.

posts.author: Priyanshu Chourasia
posts.title: GoRoutine : A way towards virtual threads.
posts.desc: Why OS threads don't scale to millions of concurrent tasks, and how Go's goroutines — a userspace, M:N-scheduled answer to the same problem 'virtual threads' solve today — got there first.
posts.intro: Long before 'virtual threads' became a buzzword in Java and other ecosystems, Go shipped an answer to the same problem: how do you run hundreds of thousands of concurrent tasks without hundreds of thousands of OS threads?
posts.content:
The problem with OS threads. An operating system thread is expensive. Each one gets a large, fixed-size stack (often 1–8 MB), a kernel-managed scheduling entry, and a context switch that has to trap into the kernel. Spawn ten thousand of them and you've burned gigabytes of memory before any of them do useful work, and the OS scheduler starts spending more time switching between threads than running your code. Threads were designed assuming there would be dozens of them per machine, not millions.


So what is a 'virtual thread'?

A virtual thread is a thread-like unit of execution that lives in userspace instead of the kernel. Instead of mapping one logical task to one OS thread, a runtime multiplexes many lightweight tasks onto a small pool of real OS threads, parking and resuming them as needed. The task gets to keep writing simple, sequential, blocking-looking code — read(), then process(), then write() — while the runtime handles the actual scheduling underneath. Java's Project Loom popularized the term 'virtual thread' for exactly this idea.


Go got there first — it just called it something else

Go shipped this model in 2009, calling its unit of concurrency a goroutine. A goroutine starts with a tiny stack — around 2 KB — that grows and shrinks dynamically as needed, instead of a fixed multi-megabyte allocation. Spawning one costs a few microseconds. It's entirely reasonable to spin up a million of them on a single machine.


The GMP scheduler

Go's runtime implements what's commonly called the GMP model:

  • G (Goroutine) — the lightweight task itself: a function, its stack, and its state.
  • M (Machine) — an actual OS thread that executes code.
  • P (Processor) — a scheduling context that holds a run queue of goroutines and is required for an M to execute Go code.

This is M:N scheduling — M goroutines multiplexed onto N OS threads, where M can be in the millions and N is typically close to the number of CPU cores. When a goroutine blocks on a channel, a mutex, or Go's own network poller, the scheduler parks it and hands the underlying thread to another runnable goroutine instead of letting that thread sit idle. When a goroutine makes a blocking syscall, the runtime can detach the M from its P and spin up a fresh M so other goroutines aren't starved.


Cooperative, but rarely feels like it

Goroutines are scheduled cooperatively at safe points — function calls, channel operations, memory allocation — rather than fully preemptively like OS threads. Since Go 1.14, the runtime can also asynchronously preempt a long-running, tight-loop goroutine that never hits a natural safe point, so a single misbehaving goroutine can't starve the whole program. In practice, you write code as if each goroutine just runs, and the scheduler quietly does the hard part.


Share memory by communicating

The other half of Go's concurrency story is channels, built on Tony Hoare's Communicating Sequential Processes (CSP). Go's own mantra puts it directly: 'Don't communicate by sharing memory; share memory by communicating.' Instead of guarding shared state with locks, goroutines pass ownership of data through a channel, and only one goroutine touches it at a time. Mutexes still exist in Go for the cases that need them, but channels are the idiomatic default for coordinating goroutines.


Same destination, different roads

Java's virtual threads deliberately preserve the classic Thread API and the thread-per-request mental model, so existing blocking code can adopt them with minimal changes — the JVM handles the mounting and unmounting onto 'carrier' OS threads underneath. Goroutines took a different road: a new keyword (go), a new primitive (channels), and a language built around CSP from day one rather than retrofitted onto an existing threading model. Both are chasing the same goal — cheap, massively concurrent, blocking-style code without the cost of one OS thread per task — they just arrived from opposite directions.
posts.footer: Goroutines and virtual threads are two implementations of the same underlying idea: userspace, M:N-scheduled concurrency. If TCP taught us how bytes move reliably between machines, goroutines and channels are a reminder that how you schedule and coordinate work within a single machine matters just as much.

posts.author: Priyanshu Chourasia
posts.title: TCP: What is it and how does it work?
posts.desc: A practical introduction to TCP — why communication protocols exist, how TCP provides reliable communication, how it fits into the TCP/IP stack, and how the OSI model helps us understand networking.
posts.intro: Computers need rules to communicate. TCP is one of those rules — a transport-layer protocol that helps devices exchange data reliably across an unreliable network.
posts.content:
What does TCP actually mean?. TCP stands for Transmission Control Protocol. Let's understand the name word by word. Transmission simply means sending or transferring something from one place, person, or thing to another. In networking, it means transferring data from one device to another. That data is usually broken into smaller pieces called packets or segments before being transmitted across the network.


What is a protocol?

A protocol is simply a set of rules that defines how something should happen. Think about traffic rules. If there were no rules, every vehicle could move however it wanted. Cars would not know when to stop, when to go, or who should have the right of way. Computer networks work in a similar way. When two devices communicate, they need agreed-upon rules for how data is sent, received, identified, acknowledged, and handled when something goes wrong. These rules are called protocols.


So, what is TCP?

TCP, or Transmission Control Protocol, is a communication protocol that allows applications on different devices to exchange data reliably over a network. TCP is connection-oriented and works at the Transport Layer. Its job is not simply to move data from one computer to another. It also makes sure that data can be delivered in the correct order and retransmitted when necessary. This is what allows applications to communicate over a network without having to handle every packet-level problem themselves.


But why do we need communication protocols?

When you type something into a search engine and press Enter, it feels like a very simple action. But behind that simple action, many different devices and systems communicate with each other. Your computer communicates with your router, the router communicates through the Internet, and eventually your request reaches servers that process it and send a response back. For all of these systems to communicate, they need common rules. Those rules are defined by networking protocols.


The problem before common standards

Imagine a world where every hardware manufacturer created its own communication rules. Suppose Company A builds computers, servers, and networking equipment and creates its own way of communicating between them. Everything from Company A works well together. Now suppose Company B creates its own hardware and its own communication system. Company B's devices also work well together, but they may not understand Company A's system.


Now imagine that you are already using Company A's hardware, but Company B has a cheaper and more powerful server. You buy the server, but discover that it cannot properly communicate with the hardware you already have because the systems follow different communication rules. This is an example of the kind of interoperability problem that networking standards were designed to address. It can also contribute to vendor lock-in, where switching from one vendor's technology to another becomes difficult or expensive.


What is vendor lock-in?

Vendor lock-in happens when an organization becomes heavily dependent on one company's technology, making it difficult or expensive to switch to another vendor. Standardized interfaces and protocols help reduce this problem by allowing products from different manufacturers to communicate using common rules.


Enter OSI

This brings us to OSI, which stands for Open Systems Interconnection. The OSI model was developed by the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) as a reference model for understanding how different networking systems communicate. The important thing to understand is that OSI is a reference model, not the Internet itself. It gives us a structured way to understand the different responsibilities involved in network communication.


Networking is complicated. Instead of treating communication as one huge process, the OSI model divides it into seven layers. Each layer has a specific responsibility and interacts with the layers around it.


The seven layers of OSI

7. Application — Provides network services to applications.

6. Presentation — Handles data representation, encoding, encryption, and compression.

5. Session — Manages communication sessions between systems.

4. Transport — Provides end-to-end transport services. This is where TCP fits conceptually.

3. Network — Handles logical addressing and routing, such as IP.

2. Data Link — Handles communication over a local network and frames.

1. Physical — Deals with the actual transmission of bits through cables, radio signals, and other physical media.


So where does TCP fit?

TCP belongs to the TCP/IP protocol suite and operates at the Transport Layer. The OSI model also has a Transport Layer, which is why we commonly describe TCP as a Layer 4 protocol. However, TCP is not a protocol that exists 'inside the OSI model'. OSI is a conceptual reference model, while TCP is an actual networking protocol used in real-world networks.


OSI vs TCP/IP

The Internet primarily uses the TCP/IP protocol suite, not the seven-layer OSI protocol stack. The OSI model is mainly useful for understanding and explaining networking concepts. In the TCP/IP architecture, the Application layer roughly covers the responsibilities of the OSI Application, Presentation, and Session layers. TCP belongs to the Transport layer, IP belongs to the Internet layer, and technologies such as Ethernet and Wi-Fi operate around the Link layer.


The bigger picture

Now we can connect everything together. When an application wants to communicate, it does not need to understand every detail of the physical network. Different protocols handle different responsibilities.

For example, an application may use HTTP or HTTPS at the application level, TCP at the transport level, and IP at the network level. Below that, Ethernet or Wi-Fi can handle communication across the local network.


You can visualize it like this:

Application     → HTTP / HTTPS
       ↓
Transport       → TCP
       ↓
Internet        → IP
       ↓
Link            → Ethernet / Wi-Fi
       ↓
Physical        → Cables / Radio Signals

Each layer and protocol has a different responsibility. Instead of one giant system trying to handle everything, networking is divided into smaller, well-defined responsibilities. This layered approach is one of the fundamental ideas that makes modern computer networking possible.


And this is where TCP becomes interesting

We now know why protocols exist, what the OSI model is, and where TCP fits. But we still have an important question: how does TCP actually make communication reliable? How does it know that data was received? What happens when a packet is lost? How does it establish a connection? How does it close one?


To answer those questions, we need to look at the TCP three-way handshake, sequence numbers, acknowledgements, flow control, congestion control, retransmission, and connection teardown.
posts.footer: Now that we understand what TCP is and why networking needs layers and protocols, the next step is to see TCP in action. We can start with the most important part: the three-way handshake — SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK — and then understand how TCP uses sequence numbers and acknowledgements to make an unreliable network feel reliable to an application.

posts.author: Priyanshu Chourasia
posts.title: Why I built a clinic ERP for single-doctor practices — and what it taught me about rebuilding software right the second time
posts.desc: The origin story behind OPD ERP — why solo practitioners are stuck between paper registers and bloated hospital software, and the v1-to-v2 rebuild that taught me when to scrap working code.
posts.intro: Solo doctors don't need a hospital ERP. They need the same journey, without the overhead.
posts.content:
The gap nobody was filling. Small clinics and solo practitioners are stuck between two bad options: paper registers and spreadsheets, or enterprise hospital ERPs built for multi-department hospitals — expensive, bloated, and mostly irrelevant to a single doctor's day. A solo practice still runs through the full patient journey — registration, appointment, queue, consultation, prescription, billing, dispensing — it just doesn't need the organizational overhead of a big hospital system on top of it. The goal for OPD ERP was something lightweight enough for a solo practitioner, but powerful enough to grow into a multi-doctor clinic, a pharmacy-integrated setup, or a diagnostic centre.


v1 → v2: scrapping working code on purpose

v1 was a working Express system with dual Prisma schemas and a proxy pattern between an apps/api and an apps/auth-api. It worked — but the split architecture meant schema duplication and duplicated auth logic every time something changed. I made the deliberate call to tear it down and rebuild as v2: a single unified NestJS backend instead of two services quietly drifting apart. Before deleting v1, I captured its full spec in PROJECT_BLUEPRINT.md so none of that institutional knowledge got lost in the rewrite. v2 was then built incrementally and transparently — bare scaffolding, then validation/forms/UI kit, then branding, then role-based dashboards, then POS, then the full business logic. Sometimes the right move is deleting code that works, because the architecture underneath it won't scale cleanly.


The journey, end to end

Walk-in / Scheduled → Registration → Appointment → Token Queue → Consultation → Prescription → Lab / Radiology / Procedure Orders → Billing / POS → Pharmacy Dispensing.


A few things make this feel like a real clinic tool instead of a CRUD demo. The token queue auto-refreshes live and drives a public waiting-room display board. One login produces five completely different apps — a receptionist gets a fast POS-style terminal, a doctor gets a consult workspace, a patient gets a portal, and admin gets a full back-office dashboard. Prescriptions come with drug-catalog search, substitution tracking, allergy flags, and auto-generated lab/radiology orders straight from the consult screen. Billing has a discount engine, multiple payment modes, and a refund audit trail. And underneath all of it sits RBAC done properly — granular resource:action permissions per endpoint, JWT access/refresh tokens with rotation and theft detection. There's even a small developer platform — a live schema explorer and module registry — a very 'built by developers, for the developers who maintain it' touch.


Decisions worth explaining

  • NestJS + Prisma, one schema — a single source of truth beat premature service-splitting at this scale.
  • TanStack Router over Next.js — file-based routing without SSR overhead the app doesn't need.
  • Role-based routing as architecture — pathless layouts per role (_dashboard, _pos, _doctor, _receptionist, _patient, _developer) instead of one dashboard with conditional rendering. Cleaner mental model, better UX per role.
  • Booking ≠ waiting — an appointment never puts a patient in the live queue; only checking them in does. A small distinction, but it's the difference between the queue reflecting who's actually waiting versus everyone with a future booking.
  • Doctor-level data scoping — a doctor should never see another doctor's patients or prescriptions, retrofitted deliberately rather than assumed.

What's not done yet

The queue currently polls — no WebSocket layer yet. There's no payment gateway integration, no multi-branch/multi-clinic scoping, and no automated test suite or CI. Some endpoints still lack auth guards and are open by default — a known gap, not swept under the rug.


Who it's for

Solo practitioners who want one tool instead of five. Small multi-doctor clinics. Pharmacy-integrated practices that want prescribe → dispense → bill without manual handoffs. Diagnostic centres that need lab/radiology/procedure order tracking.


Building this taught me the real tradeoff isn't 'ship fast' versus 'rebuild right' — it's knowing which one the current version of the problem actually needs. v1 shipped fast and taught me exactly where it would break under real weight. v2 is where that lesson got applied. Next: real-time queues, payments, and multi-clinic support.
posts.footer: OPD ERP is live at opd.codymitra.com. The pre-rewrite spec that survived the v1 deletion lives on as PROJECT_BLUEPRINT.md.

posts.author: Priyanshu Chourasia
posts.title: Account ERP Project
posts.desc: An accounting and finance ERP module — part of the same product suite as OPD ERP and CodyERP. Ledgers, invoicing, and financial reporting, currently in active development.
posts.intro: Accounting & finance ERP — in active development
posts.content:
Why another ERP module?. OPD ERP handles the clinical side of the CodyMitra suite — registration, queues, consultations, pharmacy. Money still needed a home. Account ERP is the accounting and finance module for the same product family: ledgers, invoicing, expense tracking, and financial reporting that the other apps in the suite can eventually plug into.


It's a standalone repo right now, deliberately scoped small so I can get the core accounting primitives — chart of accounts, journal entries, double-entry balancing — right before wiring it into OPD ERP's billing data or CodyERP's restaurant POS.


What's being built

  • Chart of accounts — configurable account hierarchy per business type.
  • Journal entries — double-entry bookkeeping with automatic balancing checks.
  • Invoicing — generate, send, and track invoice status.
  • Reports — P&L, balance sheet, and cash flow rolled up from the ledger.

Same stack discipline as the rest of the suite — TypeScript end to end, Postgres as the source of truth, and a schema I'm trying hard not to have to migrate twice.
posts.footer: Account ERP is in active development — code and progress live on GitHub.

posts.author: Priyanshu Chourasia
posts.title: ERP: What is it? What do I understand of it.
posts.desc: A personal take on what ERP actually means, after building two of them — the parts nobody tells you about until you're knee-deep in a schema.
posts.intro: Enterprise Resource Planning, from the inside
posts.content:
ERP, before I built one. Before OPD ERP, 'ERP' was just a word from business-school slides — Enterprise Resource Planning, some big SAP-shaped thing companies bought and complained about. After building two of them, I understand it very differently.


It's not one app — it's a shared source of truth

An ERP isn't a CRUD app with more tables. It's several apps — registration, billing, inventory, pharmacy, accounting — that all have to agree on the same state at the same time. The hard part was never the forms; it was making sure a token status change in the queue, a stock decrement in the pharmacy, and a line item in an invoice all stay consistent without three separate services quietly disagreeing.


What actually makes it 'enterprise'

  • Role-native interfaces — a receptionist, a doctor, and a pharmacist should never see the same screen. Each role needs its own workflow, not a shared dashboard with permissions hiding buttons.
  • Granular access control — resource:action permissions on every endpoint, not a single admin/user toggle.
  • Auditability — every state change (a prescription edit, a refund, a journal entry) needs a trail, because someone will eventually ask 'who changed this and when.'
  • Module boundaries that don't leak — Account ERP has to be able to read OPD ERP's billing data someday without becoming tightly coupled to it.

What I got wrong at first

I started OPD ERP thinking the schema was the whole job. It's maybe a third of it. The rest is workflow — modelling a token that moves through five real-world states, or a prescription that can be partially dispensed and later returned. That's where most of my redesigns happened, not in the database.


Account ERP is where I'm applying that lesson from day one — smaller scope, double-entry correctness before features, and a schema I'm trying not to migrate twice.
posts.footer: Case studies: OPD ERP Project and Account ERP Project.
